overview: The Alabama people belong to the Indigenous history of the southeastern woodlands, including towns around the Alabama River. Alabama is a Muskogean language, closely related to but distinct from Koasati. Long associations with Coushatta communities produced shared institutions without making the two names or languages identical.

periods.title: Towns, trade and Fort Toulouse
periods.summary: Alabama labor helped build the French Fort Toulouse in 1717. Nearby towns used river connections and European rivalry to support trade and diplomacy. French withdrawal after the 1763 settlement disrupted this relationship.

periods.title: Westward movements and new settlements
periods.summary: Alabama and Coushatta communities followed several westward routes after 1763. Villages developed in Louisiana and eastern Texas. These movements occurred over time; they were not one simultaneous departure by every family.

periods.title: The Texas reservation community
periods.summary: The Alabamas received a reservation grant in Polk County in 1854. Coushattas began joining them there in 1859 with Alabama permission, strengthening the shared community later called Alabama-Coushatta.

periods.title: Federal termination policy
periods.summary: The 1954 termination law changed the Texas community’s relationship with the federal government. The later Restoration Act explicitly addressed rights and privileges diminished or lost under that law. It did not describe the people as extinct.

periods.title: Restored federal recognition in Texas
periods.summary: The 1987 Restoration Act restored federal recognition and the trust relationship for the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas. It also restored eligibility for federal tribal services. This legal change concerned an existing community.

items.text: Eighteenth-century towns governed their affairs through a headman, elders and a war chief. Kinship connected neighboring settlements, while leaders negotiated alliances with other Indigenous towns and European powers. Political coordination grew from local institutions rather than requiring every town to surrender its autonomy.

Families linked Alabama and Coushatta towns with the French garrison through intermarriage. Shuck-Hall describes children of Indigenous women and French men receiving their mothers’ clan membership. This continuity in kinship organization complicates any simple equation between imported trade goods and the loss of community identity.

Drawing on an April 1831 census, historian Harriet Smither places Alabama households in villages on the Neches, including Peach Tree Village. Her account describes corn, beans, sweet potatoes and peas, with surplus produce sold or shared with visitors. Farming supplied households and supported exchange and hospitality.

Smither also describes seasonal hunting journeys with family members, bedding, tents and cooking equipment. Dressed skins and bear oil reached the Nacogdoches market. This account connects settled villages with mobile work and trade; it does not imply that agriculture and hunting belonged to separate kinds of people.

The tribe’s history credits Colabe, second chief during Antone’s leadership, with speaking Alabama, English, French and the Mobilian trade language. He interpreted and attended conferences. His work illustrates how multilingual knowledge supported representation and negotiation across the changing political world of nineteenth-century Texas.

The Gorman Museum catalogs a basket made by Florena Robinson in 1973 under the Alabama Coushatta affiliation. It entered the collection as a gift from Carol and Don Tallman. A named maker and dated object preserve an individual contribution to basketry; the catalog provides no archaeological findspot or manufacturing account.

In a 2021 interview, Elliot Abbey described learning around his basket-making aunts, then using single stitches and a newer wheat-stitch pattern in his own work. Abbey is Coushatta from Louisiana; his wife and children are Alabama-Coushatta. Their life in Texas shows how artistic knowledge crosses closely related communities through families.

Abbey recalled harvesting pine needles near home with his family in 2019 after new plantings made them accessible. The same report describes Gesse Bullock’s work managing prescribed burns for the tribe. Forest management helped sustain material needed by basket makers, linking a household craft with community stewardship.

Cora Sylestine, Heather K. Hardy and Timothy Montler produced the Dictionary of the Alabama Language, published in 1993. Its online form followed in 1999. Their introduction treats Alabama and Koasati as separate languages, cautioning that close relationship does not guarantee mutual understanding.

The dictionary’s pronunciation guide distinguishes short and long vowels, tone and consonant length. It gives kolbi for basket and oki for water. Its spelling guidance records differences that ordinary English spelling could obscure, making written documentation more useful to readers learning how words are pronounced.

The Briscoe Center preserves copies of three deeds concerning transfers through Texas to the Alabama Indians in 1854 to 1855, plus a record concerning one seller’s purchase. Its finding aid says the community holds the originals. These are specific documentary traces of the reservation’s creation, not evidence of an unrestricted historical homeland.

A separate history continued in Oklahoma. Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town traces its community through removal from the Southeast and continued ceremonial government near Wetumka. Its account identifies April 1939 as approval of its constitution. This institution should not be confused with the later federal restoration of the Texas tribe.

ending.text: The Alabama did not disappear when this map interval ends in 1783. Displacement led to different community histories, including Alabama-Coushatta government in Texas and Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town in Oklahoma. Their continuing institutions make an extinction date inappropriate. Federal termination and restoration in Texas concern political recognition, not the beginning or end of a people.
